narrative: Today's strongest signal comes from predator-prey and trophic-cascade work: a 24-year dataset from a semi-arid Chilean ecosystem shows owl diet specialization tracking climate-driven prey scarcity, while a Central European study finds that wolves and humans jointly, and comparably, shape deer browsing pressure on forest regeneration. Fire ecology contributes a rare long view, with lodgepole pine stands sampled 35 years after a stand-replacing fire showing aboveground nitrogen pools still accumulating while near-surface belowground pools remain flat, a slow trajectory echoed by a 12-year Argentine dataset in which post-fire vegetation recovery lags well behind pre-fire baselines. Urbanisation research is also prominent: three papers converge on the idea that cities filter but do not homogenise biological communities, from regionally distinct Mexican urban bird assemblages to eco-evolutionary feedbacks in US metropolitan landscapes to functional-trait mismatches in green-space bird communities. On invasion and symbiosis, a 37-expert horizon scan flags high-risk incoming species for the Canary Islands, metagenomic sequencing reveals unexpectedly diverse, genome-eroded Frankia symbionts inside Casuarina root nodules, and an ectomycorrhizal dominance study argues that mixed rather than single-strategy mycorrhizal communities best sustain forest tree diversity. Methodological advances worth flagging include a new R package for landscape-connectivity modelling (geohabnet) and a Bayesian framework correcting roadkill counts for imperfect carcass detection. Across evolution and biogeography, urban environments repeatedly accelerate or redirect plant adaptive trajectories, while a global analysis of 10,290 bird species finds plumage colour and pattern tracking climate gradients in ways consistent with both Gloger's and Bogert's rules operating jointly rather than competing.
